dimensions.note: This model handles FOUR distinct bearer credentials — more than any other in the suite — and that is the reason this dimension got the most attention. (1) applicationKey: .meta({ sensitive: true }), vault-sourced, never echoed. (2) The 24h account authorizationToken: header only. (3) The per-endpoint upload token from b2_get_upload_url / b2_get_upload_part_url: postBytes deliberately bypasses the shared client because upload endpoints are off-cluster, carry their own token and take a byte body; the token is set as an Authorization header and never persisted. (4) The download authorization token, which is the design decision worth recording: b2_get_download_authorization returns a token granting read access to a whole prefix for up to seven days, and it is NEVER written to a snapshot or a log. That diverges from b2-key's secretDestination pattern on purpose, and the difference is regenerability — B2 returns an application key's secret exactly once and it is lost forever if uncaptured, whereas this token can be re-minted at will, so persisting a copy would be all risk and no benefit. The guarantee is asserted in the data itself via tokenPersisted: false, not only in prose. Verified by execution across every method: the mechanical harness plants all four secrets in its fixtures and greps every snapshot and log line (step 5, OK), and a dedicated test asserts the account token never travels in a request body. Residual, documented: fileInfo is arbitrary user metadata B2 stores and returns on every read, so it lands in a snapshot verbatim — the README warns it must never hold a credential, matching the bucketInfo precedent.

Structured throughout: message templates with named placeholders and a props object, never concatenated values. Warnings are reserved for facts an operator must not miss and each names the consequence rather than the symptom — a truncated part listing says the counts are a FLOOR, a bucket with no readable bucketId says that is not evidence it has no unfinished uploads, and a rejected download authorization says the token grants nothing. The sharpest one is in the large-upload rescue path: if the upload fails AND the compensating cancel also fails, the warning states that the parts are still stored and still billed and prints the exact command to clean them up, because that is a permanent invisible charge and a generic error would leave the operator with no idea it happened. Asserted by test, not by inspection.

b2Fetch throws Error & { status, b2Code } and the model branches on the code, never on message text; postBytes reproduces that contract for the upload endpoints so a caller cannot tell which client threw. 401 unauthorized is deliberately not retried — a missing capability is not transient, and the README maps every method to the capabilities it needs. Ordering was audited method by method and the guards fire before any B2 call: the size guard runs before b2_authorize_account itself (which is class-C), and delete's destruction gate runs before authorizing too, both asserted by tests checking calls.length === 0. The compensating-transaction path is the substance here: a large upload that fails after b2_start_large_file leaves a file whose parts are billed indefinitely and are invisible in the console's file browser, so the model cancels it on failure — best-effort, in a nested try, so a failed cancel can never mask the original error. Both branches are tested.

49 tests, all mocked, plus a mechanical harness that executes every method and diffs each spec's schema keys against the keys actually written (unfinished-upload 14/14, transfer 13/13, download-auth 8/8, ALL PASS). CONVENTIONS §10 items 1-7 are covered: nested v4 auth shape, null allowed.buckets, flat v2/v3 body rejected, two-page part drain with nextPartNumber->startPartNumber renaming, page-cap truncation, exactly-one re-auth on expired_auth_token, 429 with Retry-After, non-transient 400 carrying b2Code, idempotent delete, no secret leaks. The harness was proven to bite by mutation rather than assumed, twice: stringifying the derived `bytes` field failed 10 tests with the schema-rejection message, and a schema-LEGAL semantic mutation (sha1Verified ?? false, collapsing 'not checked' into 'checked and wrong') failed exactly the two tests written to catch it. Both were reverted and the suite re-verified green. One test was itself found wrong during the build and fixed: it asserted on a ReadableStream's start() callback, which fires at Response construction, so it would have passed even if the body HAD been read; it now spies on arrayBuffer(), the call the model actually makes.

scan, download, list_parts and authorize_download are read-only and naturally repeatable. delete is idempotent per CONVENTIONS §3: a 404, or a 400 with b2Code file_not_present or no_such_file, is a success that still writes the absent tombstone. isAlreadyGone deliberately excludes bad_bucket_id — that is a configuration bug, and swallowing it would report a successful cancel of an upload still accruing storage in the bucket the caller actually meant; asserted directly. reauth is threaded through every b2Fetch call site so a long fleet scan survives the 24h token expiring mid-run. upload is NOT idempotent by nature — B2 versions every write, so re-running creates a new version — and that is documented rather than pretended away. copy_part is likewise a positional write into a specific part number.

Built against the v4 corrections in CONVENTIONS §4 rather than Backblaze's prose. The canonical client (§5) was copied byte-identical from b2-files and verified so programmatically after the copy, not by eye. All thirteen wave-3 operations are covered and were confirmed present by a mechanical grep: b2_list_unfinished_large_files, b2_get_upload_url, b2_upload_file, b2_start_large_file, b2_get_upload_part_url, b2_upload_part, b2_finish_large_file, b2_cancel_large_file, b2_list_parts, b2_copy_part, b2_download_file_by_id, b2_download_file_by_name, b2_get_download_authorization — completing the suite's coverage of all 33. Two contract details worth recording: b2_upload_file and b2_upload_part are reached via the uploadUrl B2 returns rather than by name on the cluster apiUrl, which is how that API works; and b2_list_parts is scoped by B2 to writeFiles rather than to a read capability, which the README states because a read-only key will otherwise fail on a method that looks read-only. LIVE-VERIFIED 2026-08-06: a real read-only scan across the account returned ten genuine unfinished uploads, and countParts sized them, exercising b2_list_unfinished_large_files, b2_list_parts and the pagination path against production data.

Three specs, cleanly separated by what they describe: unfinished-upload is an object B2 is billing for, transfer is the outcome of one movement, download-auth is a grant's shape. scan is a genuine factory — one execution fans out across every visible bucket and acquires the per-model lock once (CLAUDE.md rule 6). Cost is designed against: countParts is opt-in precisely because it is one class-C call per unfinished file; a pinned bucketName+bucketId skips b2_list_buckets entirely; and the large-upload path fetches b2_get_upload_part_url ONCE and reuses it across parts rather than paying a class-C call per part, asserted by test. The defining decision is the size guard: maxTransferBytes defaults to 100 MB, is checked before any B2 call including authorize, is overridable per run, and is additionally policed by a check that rejects a model-level cap above 1 GiB. A model that can stream a 40 GB restic pack file through a Deno process by accident has no business existing next to this estate; this one cannot.

Every fixture and README example uses example.com-class names and fake-but-plausible B2 identifiers (example-backup-bucket, 4a48fe8875c6214145260818, 4_zexamplelargefileid00001). Checked with particular care because this build read live output containing real bucket names, real Time Machine file paths and real 83-character file IDs — the exact circumstance in which one gets pasted into a fixture, and a mistake I made in this same session in the b2-hygiene README. The model source, the test file, the mechanical harness and the README contain no real bucket name, file path or file ID. The one real-world detail that IS published is the STRUCTURE of a B2 large-file ID (4_z<bucket>_f<file>_d<date>_m<minute>_c<cluster>_v<vol>_t<seq>), which appears in a code comment and a test because it is the justification for the instance-name hash; that is a public property of B2's ID format, not of this account, and the test's fixture IDs are synthetic.

Calibrated per CONVENTIONS §4.9 — strict where the shape is documented and observed, permissive where it is not. Byte and count fields are z.number().int(). The honest-null contract is enforced in the schema itself and its descriptions say what null MEANS, not merely that it is allowed: partCount null is 'not measured, run list_parts', never zero parts; sha1Verified null is 'NOT CHECKED', explicitly distinguished from false meaning 'computed and mismatched'. That three-state distinction is the one most likely to be flattened by a consumer, so the README tells readers to branch on === false rather than on falsiness. contentSha1 is recorded VERBATIM rather than normalised, because B2's 'none' and 'unverified:' prefixes are themselves the fact. tokenPersisted is z.literal(false) — a schema-level guarantee that the field can never carry anything else. fileInfo is held loosely (a non-object degrades to null) so an unexpected shape cannot sink a fleet scan. Field coverage is verified by execution, 1:1 in both directions across all three specs.

All three specs are lifetime 'infinite' with garbageCollection 50, matching the rest of the suite. Right for unfinished-upload, whose value is the trend — 50 versions of a per-upload part count is the series showing whether an abandoned upload is growing or was finally cancelled, and the delete tombstone needs to outlive the object it describes. Right for transfer, where a canary written on a schedule produces exactly the history you want: 50 round-trips with their SHA-1 verdicts is a readable record of whether a bucket has stayed healthy. For download-auth the cap is close to moot: each (bucket, prefix) pair keys one instance and re-minting rewrites it, so 50 versions is 50 mints of the same grant, which is a useful audit trail at negligible cost.

Seven methods covering all thirteen operations PRD §4 assigns to this model, mapped one-to-one in the README's method table. Method names follow the PRD (upload, download, authorize_download, list_parts, copy_part) rather than the §3 taxonomy, which is a deliberate and documented divergence — but delete is named delete precisely so its pre-flight check fires, since checks auto-run only for create/update/delete/action. Deliberately out of scope and stated as such: resuming a partially-completed large upload from a previous run is not modelled (the parts are visible via list_parts, but re-driving them needs the original byte source, which swamp does not persist), and the S3-compatible API remains out of scope per PRD §2 because restic uses it directly for the data plane.

Three checks, all labelled policy: credentials-present, transfer-destruction-acknowledged (appliesTo delete) and transfer-limit-sane. Their limits are documented rather than papered over. swamp never gives a check the method's inputs, so transfer-destruction-acknowledged cannot see --input allowTransferDestruction=true and is not what enforces; the real gate is assertDestructionAllowed inside execute, which sees both the input and the global argument, and both paths are tested. The check exists to fail fast when the MODEL is misconfigured. transfer-limit-sane is the one addition beyond the b2-files pattern and it is deliberate: it fires on any method, and it catches the specific bad outcome of somebody raising maxTransferBytes permanently on the model to make one large transfer work, which quietly converts a guarded validation tool into an unguarded data mover. Raising it per run is the supported path and is what the error says.

Every instance is spec-prefixed per CONVENTIONS §2, since names share one flat storage namespace across specs — asserted mechanically, along with no-clobber-within-one-execution and no use of the reserved literal 'latest'. This dimension carries the build's most important defect, and LIVE DATA is what found it. unfinishedInstanceName originally used safeFragment(fileId, 48) with no hash, on the reasoning that fileId is B2's own identifier and therefore unique. That reasoning is wrong once truncated: a real B2 large-file ID is ~83 characters of the form 4_z<bucket>_f<file>_d<date>_m<minute>_c<cluster>_v<vol>_t<seq>, and 48 characters cuts inside the date — discarding everything that distinguishes two uploads of the same file at different times, so they would reduce to one instance name and silently clobber each other on disk. That is exactly the failure that made b2-bucket's notification snapshot eat its bucket snapshot. NO TEST COULD HAVE CAUGHT IT: the mock fixture used a 25-character ID that never reached the truncation. The mock was SHORTER than reality, the mirror image of wave 2's mocks being RICHER than reality, and the same lesson. Fixed by appending a hash of the full ID, with a regression test using two realistic 83-character IDs that share their first 48 characters — verified to fail when the hash is removed.

Resources are shaped for CEL querying: scalar, introspectable fields rather than nested blobs. The questions this model exists to answer are one predicate each — ageDays > 30 && status == 'present' finds abandoned uploads worth cancelling, partBytes != null && partBytes > 0 finds the ones with measurable cost, and sha1Verified == false (not !sha1Verified) finds genuinely corrupt transfers. The nullable contract is what makes those safe, and the README spells out the trap: a !sha1Verified filter silently sweeps in every never-checked transfer alongside the actually-broken ones, which is the difference between an alert that means something and one that fires constantly. partsTruncated sits beside partCount so a consumer can tell a total from a floor.

First publish at 2026.08.06.1 — no prior version exists in the registry, confirmed by the dry run's version-drift check, so there is no compatibility surface to break. Forward-looking commitments recorded so a later change is visibly breaking rather than quietly so: the three-state sha1Verified is a contract and must not be collapsed to a boolean; partCount null means unmeasured and must not become 0; unfinished-upload instances are keyed by a hash of the full fileId, so changing the naming again would orphan every existing snapshot (as it already did once during this build, when the ten instances written under the pre-fix name had to be deleted by hand — worth remembering that an instance-naming change is a data migration, not a refactor); tokenPersisted is z.literal(false) and relaxing it would be a security regression, not a feature. Adding a field is additive; narrowing a nullable one is not.
